There are some old, traditionalists who think that any forward progress (wheels, v-hull, improved ballistic/IED protection) is sacrilege no matter what, because the tracks and inboard thrusters are being removed.  

The new versions will be much faster on land, and the same speed in the water. 

I can't tell you how many times I really disliked the decades-old design of those things. While the weapons (heavy machine gun and grenade launcher) were adequate for the vehicle's intended purpose, the turret itself was outdated, too small, optics were poor, night vision was from a bygone era (if it worked at all) and everything was already broken from the last several units that had ownership of the vehicle before me. 

The transmissions were weak, which required that the engines (the one shining star on the vehicle) needed to be detuned so the torque didn't damage gearbox internals.  

Communication systems were outdated. Four of them. That's four radios, which on their own were old but still reliable, yet were at the mercy of the unreliable electrical system in the vehicle. Even following correct vehicle startup/shutdown procedures resulted in far too many dropped connections and lost secure communications.  

Standard operating procedure was basically this: Ignore any ballistic protection that the turret/vehicle might provide and stick your head out of the turret/driver's hatch so you can see where you're going during the day, and especially at night. At night there are no functioning night-vision systems built into the vehicle that work effectively....   

Driver vision enhancement? Yeah, that's a joke. That system is a basic thermal scope that will still let you crash into something at more than 3mph. At least you can use it to see the fish underwater.... if it worked at all. 

Crew chief? Yeah, I'm up there with night vision goggles trying to see where I'm going, and relay to my driver who's just a few feet away, can't hear me because any number of communication issues has decided to pop up right as we're stepping off.  

There were some pros to the vehicle designed by a boat builder. You can hide limitless amounts of contraband in them. They are so old, there are about 17 moving parts, total.

Ever been to the beach?

Ease of maintenance is crucial. If you lose a tire or wheel, the vehicle can still move forward through obstacles. 

The current amphibious assault vehicle has two tracks, and if you lose one, you're in serious trouble. 

Additionally, the final drives on the amphibious assault vehicle are weak. A few strands of concertina wire can damage them if they get tangled up. 

The tracks are costly, and the individual track pads have a short lifespan, which means you have to break the track, unroll it, and then remove or replace the individual pads. This can be extremely frustrating, as the bolts securing the pad to the track are often rusted solid and need to be cut out with a torch, especially when your tools are missing or broken, and no one in the unit has thought to purchase impact wrenches.

Moreover, there are only a couple of people in the unit authorized to use a cutting torch, and they are usually on leave or assigned to other duties.
